answer: DeepWalk (Perozzi, Al-Rfou, Skiena, 2014) learns a latent representation Φ: V → R^{d} for each vertex by treating truncated random walks as sentences and applying a skip-gram language model. For each vertex v_i in a walk, it maximizes the log-likelihood of observing the context vertices v_{i-w},...,v_{i+w} within a window of size w, i.e. minimizes J = -log Pr({v_{i-w},...,v_{i+w}} \ v_i | Φ(v_i)), with Pr(u_k | Φ(v_j)) modeled by a softmax over the whole vertex set. Because the full softmax normalization over |V| vertices is expensive, DeepWalk uses hierarchical softmax: vertices are placed at the leaves of a binary tree (a Huffman tree built from vertex frequencies in the walks), so Pr(u_k | Φ(v_j)) becomes a product of sigmoid-based binary decisions along the path from root to u_k, reducing the cost to O(log|V|). The parameters are the embedding matrix Φ (and the internal tree node weights ψ). Training is done by stochastic gradient descent: the walks are generated online, and for each (center, context) pair the gradient of the loss with respect to Φ(v_j) and the tree node weights is computed, and the parameters are updated by a small step, Φ ← Φ − α·∂J/∂Φ, with a decaying learning rate (e.g., starting around 0.025). The derivatives are obtained by backpropagation (the chain rule applied through the hierarchical softmax path): for each binary decision on the path, the derivative of the log-sigmoid gives an error term (1 − code − σ(Φ(v_j)·ψ_node)) multiplied by the node weight (for the input embedding) or by the input embedding (for the node weight), and these per-path gradients are accumulated and applied in a single SGD update per pair. Thus DeepWalk uses SGD with analytic gradients from hierarchical-softmax backpropagation, computed on the fly for each sampled walk window.
